newsitem.title: INDIA: Agriculture not left out of India budget - Finance.
newsitem.headline: Agriculture not left out of India budget - Finance.

text.p: Indian Finance Ministry officials on Saturday dismissed criticism that the 1997/98 (April-March) budget would fail to spur agricultural growth.

"The budget is unique in the history of recent budgets as it has laid so much emphasis on agriculture liberalisation," Shankar Acharya, the Finance Ministry's chief economic advisor, told reporters in a post-budget news conference.

Acharya and other ministry officials sought to counter criticism from some that the budget, presented by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram in parliament on Friday, offered few measures to encourage an increase in agricultural output.
"There is not much to encourage agriculture in this budget," Agriculture Minister Chaturanan Mishra of the Communist Party of India (CPI) said on Friday after the budget was presented.
But Finance Ministry officials said the budget would step up outlays on agriculture, abolish controls on farm products and revive or launch commodities futures in cotton, jute and castor oil.
The budget would increase federal outlays on agriculture by 13 percent and boost spending on rural development by 15.4 percent, they told the news conference.

Chidambaram also announced increases in food and fertiliser subsidies, and increased the credit flow to agriculture by 30 percent from 1996/97 levels, they said. "The budget has provided for stronger rural credit," Acharya said.
The ministry's economic adviser welcomed an increase in allocation for irrigation facilities to 13 billion rupees ($363 million) from nine billion.
"Irrigation is a key constraint for agricultural production. That has been very much addressed," Acharya said.

Montek Singh Ahluwalia, the highest ranking civil servant in the Finance Ministry said a proposal to set up a global castor oil futures exchange and to resume domestic futures in ginned cotton and jute goods was a rational policy decision.
Futures trading will stabilise prices rather than drive them down, Ahluwalia said. "Most people think that regulated futures market improve market conditions," he said. ($1 = 35.9 rupees)
